question: Under general contract law principles applicable to real estate offers, what is the legal effect of a counteroffer?
choice_a: It operates as a rejection of the original offer and proposes new terms -- the original offer can no longer be accepted unless the offeror renews it
choice_b: It has no legal effect and the original offer remains open regardless of the counteroffer
choice_c: It automatically becomes a binding contract the moment it is made, without any acceptance
choice_d: It extends the original offer's acceptance deadline automatically
explanation: Under the common-law 'mirror image' rule, an acceptance must match the offer's terms exactly. A counteroffer instead rejects the original offer and substitutes new terms, terminating the offeree's power to accept the original offer unless the offeror chooses to renew it.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general contract-law curriculum content (offer and acceptance)

question: An offeror who has made an offer to sell real property, but has not yet received an acceptance, generally may:
choice_a: Revoke the offer at any time before the offeree communicates acceptance, unless the offer is an option supported by separate consideration or is otherwise made irrevocable
choice_b: Never revoke the offer once it has been communicated to the offeree, under any circumstances
choice_c: Revoke the offer only with a court order
choice_d: Revoke the offer only if the offeree has not yet read it
explanation: As a general rule, an offer is freely revocable by the offeror at any time before acceptance is communicated, unless it is an option contract (supported by separate consideration) or otherwise made irrevocable -- an offeree's mere knowledge of the offer does not itself bar revocation.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general contract-law curriculum content (revocation of offer)

question: Under the common-law 'mailbox rule,' when is an acceptance sent by mail generally considered effective?
choice_a: Upon proper dispatch (mailing) of the acceptance, not upon the offeror's actual receipt of it
choice_b: Only upon the offeror's actual receipt and reading of the acceptance
choice_c: Only after the offeror confirms receipt by telephone
choice_d: Acceptance sent by mail is never effective; it must be delivered in person
explanation: The mailbox rule provides that a properly addressed and dispatched acceptance is effective upon mailing, not upon the offeror's actual receipt -- distinguishing acceptance from revocation, which is generally effective only upon receipt.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general contract-law curriculum content (mailbox rule)

question: For a contract to be supported by valid consideration, courts generally require:
choice_a: Something of legally sufficient value bargained for and exchanged between the parties -- courts generally do not weigh whether the values exchanged are exactly equal
choice_b: That both parties exchange items of precisely equal market value
choice_c: That consideration be paid entirely in cash
choice_d: That consideration total at least $500 to be legally enforceable
explanation: Consideration requires only legal sufficiency -- something of value bargained for in exchange for a promise -- not equivalence in economic value; courts generally do not second-guess the adequacy of a bargain freely made between competent parties.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general contract-law curriculum content (consideration)

question: Why is 'past consideration' -- a benefit or act that occurred before the promise it supposedly supports -- generally not valid consideration for a new contract?
choice_a: Because valid consideration must be given in exchange for the current promise; something already done before the promise was made was not bargained for as part of this exchange
choice_b: Because past consideration is only invalid in real estate transactions, not other types of contracts
choice_c: Because past consideration must always be recorded with the county clerk to count as valid
choice_d: Past consideration is treated exactly the same as present consideration under New York law
explanation: Consideration must be given in exchange for the promise it supports. An act or benefit that already occurred before the promise was made was not bargained for as part of that exchange, so it generally cannot serve as consideration for a later promise.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general contract-law curriculum content (past consideration)

question: A contract entered into by a minor (a person under the age of majority) for the purchase of real property is generally:
choice_a: Voidable at the minor's election -- the minor may disaffirm the contract, though failing to disaffirm within a reasonable time after reaching the age of majority can amount to ratification
choice_b: Automatically void from inception, with no possibility of enforcement by either party
choice_c: Fully binding on the minor exactly as it would be on an adult, with no special protection
choice_d: Enforceable against the minor only if a parent countersigns, and otherwise void
explanation: A minor's contract is generally voidable, not void -- the minor holds the right to disaffirm it, but if the minor does not disaffirm within a reasonable time after reaching the age of majority (18 in New York), the failure to act can amount to ratification of the contract.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (capacity of minors); age of majority per General Obligations Law Section 3-101 is 18

question: A contract entered into by a person previously adjudicated (by court order) to be mentally incompetent is generally treated as:
choice_a: Void, because a judicially adjudicated incompetent lacks legal capacity to contract at all -- this differs from a person who is impaired but has not been adjudicated incompetent, whose contract is typically only voidable
choice_b: Fully valid and enforceable regardless of the adjudication
choice_c: Automatically ratified the moment the person's guardian is appointed
choice_d: Treated identically, in every respect, to a minor's contract
explanation: A contract signed by a person already judicially adjudicated incompetent is generally void, since that person has no legal capacity to contract; by contrast, a contract with a person who is impaired but not yet adjudicated incompetent is typically only voidable at that person's election.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (capacity -- mental incompetence)

question: A 'mutual mistake' that can justify rescission of a real estate contract occurs when:
choice_a: Both parties share the same erroneous belief about a material, existing fact central to the bargain (for example, both mistakenly believing a parcel includes acreage it does not actually include)
choice_b: Only the seller misunderstands a material fact
choice_c: Only the buyer misunderstands a material fact
choice_d: Either party later simply changes their mind about wanting the property
explanation: A mutual mistake exists when both parties share the same erroneous belief about a material, existing fact underlying the bargain -- a ground for rescission distinct from mere buyer's or seller's remorse, which involves no factual error at all.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (mutual mistake)

question: A 'unilateral mistake,' where only one party misunderstands a material fact, generally:
choice_a: Does not by itself excuse performance or void the contract, unless the other party knew or should have known of the mistake, or enforcement would be unconscionable
choice_b: Always allows the mistaken party to rescind the contract, with no further showing required
choice_c: Automatically transfers liability for the mistake to the real estate broker
choice_d: Has the identical legal effect as a mutual mistake in every case
explanation: A unilateral mistake by only one party is generally not, by itself, grounds to avoid a contract -- courts typically require a showing that the other party knew or should have known of the error, or that enforcement would be unconscionable, before granting relief.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (unilateral mistake)

question: To establish common-law fraudulent misrepresentation sufficient to rescind a real estate contract, a plaintiff generally must show:
choice_a: A false representation of a material fact, made with knowledge of its falsity (or reckless disregard for the truth) and intent to induce reliance, that the other party justifiably relied on to their detriment
choice_b: Only that a statement made during negotiations later turned out to be incorrect, regardless of the speaker's knowledge or intent
choice_c: That the seller's attorney, rather than the seller, personally made the statement
choice_d: That the buyer independently verified the statement was false before relying on it
explanation: Fraudulent misrepresentation requires a false statement of material fact, knowledge of its falsity (or reckless disregard for the truth), intent to induce reliance, and justifiable reliance causing damage -- a materially higher bar than merely being wrong about something.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (fraudulent misrepresentation)

question: Unlike fraudulent misrepresentation, 'innocent misrepresentation' -- a false statement of material fact made without knowledge of its falsity or intent to deceive -- typically entitles the injured party to:
choice_a: Rescission of the contract to undo the transaction, generally without an award of punitive or fraud-based damages
choice_b: Criminal prosecution of the person who made the statement
choice_c: Nothing at all, because only intentional fraud has any legal consequence
choice_d: Automatic specific performance forcing the transaction to close on the original terms
explanation: Innocent misrepresentation lacks the scienter (knowledge of falsity/intent to deceive) required for fraud, but a false material statement can still support rescission to unwind the deal, even though the more punitive fraud-based damages generally are not available.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (innocent vs. fraudulent misrepresentation)

question: As a general rule, contract rights (such as a buyer's rights under a purchase contract) are:
choice_a: Freely assignable to a third party unless the contract prohibits assignment, the assignment would materially change the other party's duty or risk, or public policy/statute bars it
choice_b: Never assignable under any circumstances without a court order
choice_c: Assignable only if the assignee is a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Automatically void the moment any attempt to assign is made
explanation: Contract rights are generally freely assignable absent a prohibition in the contract itself, a material change to the obligor's duty or risk, or a statutory/public-policy bar -- freedom of assignment is the default rule, not the exception.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (assignment)

question: If a purchase contract contains a clause prohibiting assignment without the seller's written consent, and the buyer assigns the contract anyway without obtaining that consent:
choice_a: The assignment can constitute a breach of the contract, and the seller may have grounds to refuse to recognize the assignee or to treat the original buyer as in default
choice_b: The clause has no legal effect and is automatically unenforceable in New York
choice_c: The assignment is automatically valid and the seller must proceed with the assignee regardless of the clause
choice_d: The assignment converts the purchase contract into a lease
explanation: An anti-assignment clause is generally enforceable; assigning the contract in violation of it can constitute a breach, giving the seller grounds to refuse to recognize the assignee and to hold the original buyer responsible under the contract.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (non-assignment clauses)

question: How does a 'novation' differ from an ordinary assignment of contract rights?
choice_a: A novation substitutes a new party for an original party with the other party's consent and completely releases the original party from further liability, whereas an assignment generally does not, by itself, release the assignor from its own obligations
choice_b: A novation and an assignment are legally identical concepts with no meaningful difference
choice_c: A novation can occur without the consent of the remaining original party, unlike an assignment
choice_d: A novation only applies to lease contracts, never to purchase contracts
explanation: Unlike an assignment (which transfers rights but generally leaves the assignor still liable unless separately released), a novation is a new agreement, requiring the consent of the remaining party, that substitutes a new party in place of an original one and discharges the original party entirely.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (novation vs. assignment)

question: Compensatory (expectation) damages for breach of a real estate contract are generally intended to:
choice_a: Put the non-breaching party in the position they would have occupied had the contract been fully performed -- for example, the difference between the contract price and the property's fair market value
choice_b: Punish the breaching party beyond any actual loss suffered
choice_c: Return only the exact dollar amount of the deposit, regardless of any other loss
choice_d: Award the broker's commission directly to the non-breaching party as damages
explanation: Compensatory damages are measured by the non-breaching party's actual loss -- placing that party, so far as money can, in the position they would have occupied had the contract been performed -- rather than punishing the breaching party.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (compensatory/expectation damages)

question: Courts are especially willing to order 'specific performance' -- compelling the breaching party to actually complete the transaction -- in real estate contract disputes because:
choice_a: Real property is generally considered legally unique, so money damages are often viewed as an inadequate substitute for the particular parcel bargained for
choice_b: Specific performance is the only remedy ever available for breach of a real estate contract
choice_c: New York statute mandates specific performance automatically in every residential sale dispute
choice_d: Money damages are always easier for courts to calculate in real estate cases than in other contract disputes
explanation: Because each parcel of real property is treated as legally unique, New York courts have long recognized specific performance as an available equitable remedy in real estate disputes where a valid, enforceable contract exists and the moving party was ready, willing, and able to perform -- since money damages may not adequately substitute for that particular property.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY case-law principle (specific performance and the uniqueness of real property)

question: When a New York residential purchase contract contains a liquidated damages clause designating the buyer's down payment as the seller's sole remedy for buyer default, a seller who wishes to retain that down payment upon the buyer's default generally must show:
choice_a: That the seller was ready, willing, and able to convey marketable title on the closing date (particularly where time was of the essence) and otherwise performed the seller's own obligations under the contract
choice_b: Nothing further -- the seller may keep the deposit automatically upon any buyer delay, regardless of the seller's own performance
choice_c: That the seller has already resold the property to someone else at a higher price
choice_d: That the buyer's attorney has consented in writing to the forfeiture
explanation: To retain a down payment as liquidated damages, a New York seller generally must show the seller's own performance was not the problem -- that the seller was ready, willing, and able to deliver marketable title on the closing date -- since a seller who could not have closed anyway is not entitled to keep the deposit for the buyer's default.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY case-law principle (liquidated damages/down payment forfeiture upon buyer default)

question: 'Anticipatory breach' (or anticipatory repudiation) occurs when:
choice_a: One party clearly indicates, before the time set for performance, that they will not perform their contractual obligations -- allowing the other party to treat the contract as breached immediately rather than waiting for the performance date
choice_b: A party fails to perform, but only after the agreed performance date has already passed
choice_c: Both parties agree in advance to cancel the contract by mutual consent
choice_d: A contract is breached but neither party is aware of it
explanation: Anticipatory breach occurs when a party unequivocally communicates, before performance is due, an intent not to perform -- the non-breaching party need not wait for the performance date to pass and may treat the contract as breached and pursue remedies immediately.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (anticipatory breach/repudiation)

question: Rescission, as a contract remedy, is intended to:
choice_a: Unwind the transaction and restore both parties, as nearly as possible, to the positions they occupied before the contract was made
choice_b: Force the breaching party to complete performance exactly as originally agreed
choice_c: Award the non-breaching party money damages equal to lost future profits
choice_d: Permanently bar either party from ever contracting with each other again
explanation: Rescission is an equitable remedy that cancels the contract and restores the parties, so far as practicable, to their pre-contract positions -- distinct from specific performance (which enforces the deal) or compensatory damages (which pays for the loss while leaving the contract intact).
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (rescission)

question: A 'bilateral contract' is one in which:
choice_a: Both parties exchange mutual promises of future performance -- for example, a buyer's promise to pay the price in exchange for a seller's promise to convey title
choice_b: Only one party makes any promise at all, and the other party need only perform to accept
choice_c: The contract must be signed by exactly two witnesses
choice_d: The contract involves exactly two parcels of real property
explanation: A bilateral contract is formed by an exchange of mutual promises -- each party is both a promisor and a promisee -- which describes the typical real estate purchase contract, where the buyer promises to pay and the seller promises to convey.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (bilateral contracts)

question: A 'unilateral contract,' by contrast to a bilateral contract, is one in which:
choice_a: One party makes a promise that can only be accepted by the other party's actual performance of the requested act, rather than by a reciprocal promise
choice_b: Both parties must sign in the presence of a notary for the contract to exist
choice_c: The contract automatically terminates after one calendar year
choice_d: Only one party is bound while the other party has no obligations whatsoever, even after accepting
explanation: In a unilateral contract, only one party makes a promise, and acceptance occurs through the other party's actual performance of the requested act (rather than a return promise) -- an open listing under which a broker earns commission only by actually producing a buyer is a commonly cited example.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (unilateral contracts)

question: An 'express contract' is distinguished from an 'implied-in-fact contract' in that:
choice_a: An express contract's terms are stated explicitly, in words (oral or written), while an implied-in-fact contract's terms are inferred from the parties' conduct and the surrounding circumstances
choice_b: An implied-in-fact contract can never be legally enforceable
choice_c: An express contract must always be for the sale of real property
choice_d: There is no legal distinction between the two
explanation: An express contract's terms are explicitly stated by the parties, whereas an implied-in-fact contract's terms are inferred from the parties' conduct and the circumstances of their dealings -- both are enforceable, but a real estate sale contract must still separately satisfy the statute of frauds in writing.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (express vs. implied-in-fact contracts)

question: A 'condition precedent,' such as a mortgage contingency or an attorney approval provision, is best described as:
choice_a: An event that must occur (or be satisfied or waived) before a party's obligation to perform under the contract becomes absolute
choice_b: A clause that has no effect on when a party's performance obligation arises
choice_c: A penalty imposed on a party who closes early
choice_d: A condition that can only be included in commercial, never residential, contracts
explanation: A condition precedent is an event that must occur, be satisfied, or be waived before a party's duty to perform becomes absolute -- a mortgage contingency and an attorney approval clause are both classic real estate examples of conditions precedent to the buyer's or either party's binding obligation to close.
source_note: hedge: standard general contract-law curriculum content (conditions precedent)

question: Under General Obligations Law Section 5-703(1), if a deed is signed on the grantor's behalf by an agent rather than the grantor personally, what does the statute require regarding that agent's authority?
choice_a: The agent's authority to sign the conveyance must itself be in writing -- an oral authorization to sign a deed on someone else's behalf is not sufficient
choice_b: The agent needs no written authorization at all, as long as the grantor later verbally confirms the sale
choice_c: Only a licensed real estate broker may ever sign a deed as an agent for the grantor
choice_d: An agent may never sign a deed on a grantor's behalf under any circumstances in New York
explanation: GOL Section 5-703(1) requires that a conveyance be subscribed by the grantor or by the grantor's lawful agent, but only where that agent is 'thereunto authorized by writing' -- an oral authorization to sign a deed on the grantor's behalf does not satisfy the statute.
source_note: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(1) (Statute of frauds -- conveyances and agent authorization)

question: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(2) requires that a contract or memorandum for the sale of real property, to satisfy the statute of frauds, must be signed by the party to be charged and must also:
choice_a: Express the consideration for the transaction, in addition to being in writing and signed
choice_b: Be filed with the Department of State before the parties sign
choice_c: Be witnessed by a licensed real estate broker
choice_d: Contain no reference to price or consideration at all
explanation: GOL Section 5-703(2) requires that a contract (or note/memorandum of it) for the sale of real property be in writing, expressing the consideration, and signed by the party to be charged -- a bare unsigned writing, or one omitting the consideration, does not satisfy the statute.
source_note: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(2) (Statute of frauds -- sale contracts must express consideration)

question: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(4) preserves what important exception to the real property statute of frauds?
choice_a: It preserves the power of courts of equity to compel specific performance of an oral agreement in cases of part performance, despite the general writing requirement
choice_b: It eliminates any possibility of enforcing an oral real estate agreement under any circumstances
choice_c: It requires that all real estate contracts be fully performed within thirty days or become void
choice_d: It applies only to contracts for the sale of personal property, not real property
explanation: GOL Section 5-703(4) expressly preserves courts of equity's power to compel specific performance of an agreement despite the absence of a writing, where the party seeking enforcement has partly performed in reliance on the oral agreement -- the 'part performance' doctrine.
source_note: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(4) (Statute of frauds -- part performance exception)

question: Under General Obligations Law Section 5-703(2), which type of leasing arrangement is exempt from the requirement that it be in writing to be enforceable?
choice_a: A lease for a term not longer than one year
choice_b: Every residential lease, regardless of the term length
choice_c: No lease is ever exempt -- all leases in New York must be in writing
choice_d: Only commercial leases are exempt, never residential leases
explanation: GOL Section 5-703(2) applies its writing requirement to a leasing 'for a longer period than one year' -- meaning a lease for a term of one year or less falls outside the statute of frauds and can be enforceable even if made orally.
source_note: General Obligations Law Section 5-703(2) (Statute of frauds -- leases of one year or less exempt)

question: Which of the following is generally required for a deed to be valid and effective to convey title, as distinct from the separate requirements for recording the deed?
choice_a: A competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, a granting clause/words of conveyance, an adequate legal description of the property, and delivery of the deed to (and acceptance by) the grantee
choice_b: Recording with the county clerk, without which the deed has no effect even between the grantor and grantee
choice_c: Approval by the local board of Realtors
choice_d: A title insurance policy issued simultaneously with the deed
explanation: A valid deed requires a competent grantor, an identifiable grantee, operative words of conveyance, an adequate legal description, and delivery to and acceptance by the grantee -- a deed is valid and effective between grantor and grantee without recording; recording instead protects priority against subsequent purchasers and creditors.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content (essential elements of a valid deed)

question: As between the grantor and grantee, title to real property generally passes upon:
choice_a: Delivery of the deed to the grantee (or the grantee's agent) with the grantor's intent to presently convey, and the grantee's acceptance -- not merely upon the grantor signing the deed or the deed later being recorded
choice_b: The date the deed is recorded with the county clerk, regardless of when it was delivered
choice_c: The date the grantor signs the deed, regardless of whether it was ever delivered
choice_d: The date the purchase contract was originally signed, months before closing
explanation: Title passes when the deed is delivered with the grantor's present intent to convey and is accepted by the grantee -- signing alone, without delivery and acceptance, does not transfer title, and recording is a separate act that protects priority rather than itself transferring title.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content (delivery and acceptance of a deed)

question: A deed reciting nominal consideration, such as '$1.00 and other good and valuable consideration,' is:
choice_a: Still generally valid -- the consideration recital in a deed serves an evidentiary/formal purpose, and deeds are commonly given for gift, family, or estate-planning transfers where the stated price is not the property's full fair market value
choice_b: Automatically void because real consideration equal to fair market value must always be stated
choice_c: Only valid if the parties are complete strangers with no prior relationship
choice_d: Prohibited under New York law in all circumstances
explanation: A deed's consideration recital serves a largely formal and evidentiary function; nominal consideration ('$1.00 and other good and valuable consideration') is commonly and validly used for gifts, family transfers, and estate-planning conveyances where no full-value price is actually being paid.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content (nominal consideration in deeds)

question: Under the doctrine of 'merger by deed,' what generally happens to the terms of the purchase contract once the deed is delivered and accepted at closing?
choice_a: Contract provisions relating to the conveyance of title are generally merged into (and extinguished by) the deed, so that after closing the parties typically may sue only on the deed's covenants, unless the contract expressly provided that specific obligations would survive closing
choice_b: The purchase contract remains fully, independently enforceable forever, with the deed adding nothing to it
choice_c: The deed is void once the contract is signed, because only one of the two documents can have legal effect
choice_d: Merger applies only to commercial transactions, never to residential closings in New York
explanation: Under New York's expansively applied merger-by-deed doctrine, contract provisions concerning the conveyance itself are generally merged into and extinguished by the deed at closing; parties who want a specific obligation (such as a post-closing repair promise) to remain enforceable must expressly state in the contract that it survives closing.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY merger-by-deed doctrine; parties commonly add express survival clauses to preserve specific obligations post-closing

question: An 'executor's deed,' used when a decedent's estate conveys real property, typically:
choice_a: Warrants only that the executor has authority to convey and has not personally encumbered the title, without warranting the full chain of title that predates the decedent's ownership
choice_b: Provides the same full covenants of title as a deed with full covenants and warranty
choice_c: May only be used when the decedent died without a will
choice_d: Requires no court or fiduciary appointment to be valid
explanation: An executor's deed is used when the personal representative of a decedent's estate conveys property under the will or intestacy laws; it typically carries only a limited warranty -- that the executor has authority to convey and has not personally created any encumbrance -- without warranting the earlier chain of title.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY real estate practice/conveyancing sources (executor's deed)

question: A referee's deed conveying property sold in a mortgage foreclosure action differs from a referee's deed in a partition action in that:
choice_a: The foreclosure referee's deed conveys property sold pursuant to a foreclosure judgment to satisfy a mortgage debt, while the partition referee's deed conveys property sold pursuant to a judgment dividing (or selling and dividing the proceeds of) jointly owned property among co-owners -- in both cases the referee acts as a court officer and gives no personal warranty of title
choice_b: There is no real difference -- the two terms refer to identical proceedings under different names
choice_c: A partition referee's deed can only be issued when all co-owners are deceased
choice_d: A foreclosure referee personally warrants full title, unlike a partition referee
explanation: Both are court-supervised conveyances issued by a court-appointed referee acting under a judgment (foreclosure of a mortgage debt in one case, division/sale of jointly owned property among co-owners in the other), and in neither case does the referee personally warrant title -- the referee acts as a court officer, not as an owner with a personal stake in the property.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY real estate practice/conveyancing sources (referee's deed -- foreclosure vs. partition)

question: A 'correction deed' (or corrective deed) is used to:
choice_a: Fix an error in a previously recorded deed, such as a misspelled name or an incorrect legal description, by referencing the original deed and stating the correction
choice_b: Transfer property for the first time between unrelated strangers, in place of a bargain and sale deed
choice_c: Convey property specifically and only in a foreclosure sale
choice_d: Permanently revoke a previously delivered deed and restore title to the original grantor
explanation: A correction deed does not convey new title -- it corrects an error, such as a misspelled name, an incorrect legal description, or a wrong vesting designation, in a previously recorded deed, by referencing the original deed and stating the specific correction.
source_note: hedge: well-corroborated NY real estate practice/conveyancing sources (correction/corrective deed)

question: 'Actual notice,' as opposed to constructive or inquiry notice, refers to:
choice_a: Real, direct knowledge a party actually has of a prior conveyance or claim -- for example, being told about it directly or personally observing it
choice_b: Knowledge automatically imputed to every purchaser the moment any document is recorded anywhere in the state
choice_c: Knowledge that only a court, and never a private party, can be charged with
choice_d: Notice that must be published in a newspaper to have any legal effect
explanation: Actual notice is real, direct knowledge -- a party who is personally told about a prior unrecorded conveyance, or who personally observes evidence of it, has actual notice, which alone can defeat that party's claim to be a good-faith purchaser without notice under RPL Section 291.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content (actual notice)

question: 'Constructive notice' under New York's recording system refers to:
choice_a: Notice imputed by law to all persons once a conveyance is properly recorded, regardless of whether a subsequent purchaser actually searched the record or had personal knowledge
choice_b: Notice that requires the buyer to have personally spoken with the prior grantee
choice_c: Notice that only applies to mortgages, never to deeds
choice_d: Notice that expires automatically after one year
explanation: Once a conveyance is properly recorded, the law imputes constructive notice of it to the world -- a later purchaser is charged with knowledge of what a title search of the public record would have revealed, whether or not that purchaser actually performed the search.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content, consistent with RPL Article 9 Section 291's recording scheme (constructive notice)

question: 'Inquiry notice' can arise, for example, when:
choice_a: A prospective buyer observes that someone other than the record owner is in visible possession of the property, a circumstance that would prompt a reasonably diligent buyer to investigate further -- the buyer may be charged with whatever facts a reasonable inquiry would have revealed
choice_b: A deed has simply been recorded in the correct county clerk's office
choice_c: The buyer has actually read the recorded deed personally
choice_d: The seller mentions the sale price to a neighbor
explanation: Inquiry notice arises when circumstances -- such as someone other than the record owner being in visible possession -- would prompt a reasonably diligent buyer to investigate further; the buyer is then charged with whatever facts that reasonable investigation would have uncovered, even without actual or recorded (constructive) notice.
source_note: hedge: standard, well-corroborated general property-law curriculum content (inquiry notice)

question: According to DOS Legal Memorandum LI04, real estate brokers and salespersons may generally prepare a purchase contract using:
choice_a: A simple, fill-in-the-blank form -- ideally one jointly approved by local bar and Realtor associations -- completing straightforward, non-legal fields such as names, price, and property description, without inserting legally complex or negotiated provisions
choice_b: Any custom legal language the broker personally drafts, with no restriction, so long as the client consents
choice_c: A form that need not disclose that it is a legally binding document
choice_d: No written contract at all -- brokers are prohibited from any involvement in contract preparation
explanation: DOS Legal Memorandum LI04 permits brokers/salespersons to complete simple, fill-in-the-blank contract forms -- particularly ones jointly approved by bar and Realtor associations -- filling in non-legal details such as names, price, dates, and property description, but bars them from inserting provisions requiring legal expertise or giving legal advice.
source_note: DOS Legal Memorandum LI04 (Real Estate Brokers and Salespersons and the Unauthorized Practice of Law)

question: Per DOS Legal Memorandum LI04, what is one specific safeguard that helps protect a broker who fills in a purchase contract form from a charge of unauthorized practice of law?
choice_a: Including a clause making the contract subject to the approval of each party's respective attorney
choice_b: Requiring the broker, rather than either party's attorney, to give the final legal opinion on the contract
choice_c: Omitting the sale price from the written contract entirely
choice_d: Having the broker personally notarize the contract
explanation: LI04 identifies an attorney approval clause -- making the broker-prepared contract subject to the approval of each party's own attorney -- as a specific safeguard that helps protect the broker from a charge of engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
source_note: DOS Legal Memorandum LI04 (Real Estate Brokers and Salespersons and the Unauthorized Practice of Law -- attorney approval clause)
